learn.b: A noun is a person, place, thing, or idea. In 'The dog ran to the park', dog and park are nouns.
A verb tells what someone does or is. In 'Mia jumps high', jumps is the verb. Past tense often ends in -ed, like jumped.
An adjective tells more about a noun. In 'a red ball', red is the adjective. It can tell color, size, or how many.

qs.q: Which word is a noun in: The cat sleeps on the sofa?
qs.why: A sofa is a thing, so it is a noun.

qs.q: Which word is a verb in: Tom kicks the ball?
qs.why: Kicks is the action Tom does.

qs.q: Which word is an adjective in: She wore a yellow hat?
qs.why: Yellow describes the hat.

qs.q: What is the past tense of walk?
qs.why: Add -ed to walk to show it happened already.

qs.q: A noun can be a place, like school.
qs.why: Nouns name people, places, things, or ideas.

qs.q: Match each word to its type
Put the words in order to make a sentence

learn.b: The main idea is what a text is mostly about. Details are small facts that support it. A text about bees might have the main idea 'Bees help flowers grow'.
Characters are the people or animals in a story. The setting is where and when it happens. A story set in a dark forest at night feels different from one at a beach.
Most stories have a beginning that introduces the problem, a middle where things happen, and an end where the problem is solved.

qs.q: What is the main idea of a text?
qs.why: The main idea is the big point of the whole text.

qs.q: Who are the characters in a story?
o: The people or animals in it
qs.why: Characters are the people or animals the story is about.

qs.q: What does the setting of a story tell you?
qs.why: Setting means the place and time.

qs.q: Which part of a story solves the problem?
qs.why: The problem is usually solved at the end.

qs.q: Details in a text help support the main idea.
qs.why: Details give facts that explain the main idea.

qs.q: Match each story word to its meaning
Put these story parts in order

learn.b: Synonyms mean almost the same, like big and large. Antonyms mean the opposite, like hot and cold.
A prefix goes at the start of a word and changes its meaning. Un- means not, so unhappy means not happy. Re- means again, so reread means read again.
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings, like to, too, and two, or their and there.

qs.q: Which word is a synonym for happy?
qs.why: Glad and happy mean almost the same.

qs.q: Which word is an antonym of hot?
qs.why: Cold is the opposite of hot.

qs.q: What does the prefix un- mean in unlock?
qs.why: Unlock means to undo locking.

qs.q: What does redo mean?
qs.why: The prefix re- means again.

qs.q: The words 'see' and 'sea' are homophones.
qs.why: They sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.

qs.q: Match each word to its antonym
Put the animals from smallest to largest

learn.b: A sentence starts with a capital letter, ends with punctuation, and tells a whole idea. 'The bird sings.' is a sentence. 'The bird' is not.
Use a period for a statement, a question mark for a question, and an exclamation mark for strong feeling. Example: Where is my bag?
Put commas between three or more things in a list. Example: I packed apples, grapes, and bread.

qs.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
qs.why: It starts with a capital letter and ends with a period.

qs.q: Which end mark goes after: Where do you live
qs.why: A question needs a question mark.

qs.q: Which sentence uses commas in a list correctly?
o: I like red, blue, and green.
I like, red blue and green.
I like red blue, and, green.
qs.why: Commas separate the items in the list.

qs.q: Which word should be capitalized?
qs.why: Days of the week are capitalized.

qs.q: 'Ran to the store' is a complete sentence.
qs.why: It has no subject, so it does not say who ran.

qs.q: Match each sentence to its end mark
Put the writing steps in order

learn.b: An adverb tells how, when, or where something happens. In 'She ran quickly', quickly tells how she ran. Many adverbs end in -ly.
A pronoun takes the place of a noun, like he, she, it, they, or we. 'Sam is tall. He plays basketball.' He replaces Sam.
Past tense tells what already happened, present tense what happens now, and future tense what will happen. Example: walked, walk, will walk.

qs.q: Which word is an adverb in: The turtle moved slowly?
qs.why: Slowly tells how the turtle moved.

qs.q: Which pronoun can replace 'Maria and I'?
qs.why: We means the speaker plus another person.

qs.q: Which sentence is in future tense?
qs.why: Will plus a verb shows the future.

qs.q: Choose the correct past tense of 'go'.
qs.why: Go is irregular, and its past tense is went.

qs.q: A pronoun takes the place of a noun.
qs.why: Pronouns like he and they replace nouns.

qs.q: Match each word to its type
Put the steps to turn 'jump' into past tense in order

learn.b: The theme is the lesson or message of a story, like 'honesty matters' or 'never give up'. You find it by looking at what the characters learn.
First person uses I and we, and the narrator is in the story. Third person uses he, she, and they, and the narrator tells about others.
When you answer a question about a text, point to words in the text that prove your answer. This is called text evidence.

qs.q: What is the theme of a story?
qs.why: Theme is the big lesson of the story.

qs.q: Which sentence is in first person?
qs.why: First person uses I.

qs.q: Which sentence is in third person?
qs.why: Third person talks about others, using he, she, or names.

qs.q: What is text evidence?
o: Words from the text that support your answer
qs.why: Evidence comes directly from the text.

qs.q: A story's theme is always stated in the first sentence.
qs.why: Readers usually figure out the theme from what happens.

qs.q: Match each reading term to its meaning
Put these steps for answering a question in order
items: Find the part of the text

learn.b: When you meet a new word, look at the words around it for hints. In 'The enormous elephant was huge', the word huge helps you guess enormous means very big.
A suffix goes at the end of a word. -ful means full of, so joyful means full of joy. -less means without, so hopeless means without hope.
A simile compares two things using like or as: 'as quick as a fox'. A metaphor says one thing is another: 'The classroom was a zoo'.

qs.q: What does the suffix -less mean in 'careless'?
qs.why: -less means without, so careless means without care.

qs.q: Which sentence has a simile?
qs.why: A simile uses the word like or as.

qs.q: Which sentence has a metaphor?
o: The room was as hot as an oven.
qs.why: A metaphor says one thing is another without like or as.

qs.q: What does 'timid' mean: The timid mouse hid because it was shy and scared.
qs.why: The clue words shy and scared explain timid.

qs.q: The suffix -ful means full of.
qs.why: Helpful means full of help.

qs.q: Match each word to its meaning
Put these words from weakest to strongest feeling

learn.b: In an opinion piece, you state what you think and give reasons. Start with your opinion, add reasons with facts, and end with a closing sentence.
A fact can be proven, like 'Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius'. An opinion tells what someone thinks, like 'Winter is the best season'.
Use quotation marks around a speaker's exact words. Example: Mom said, "Dinner is ready." The comma and period go inside the quotes.

qs.q: Which sentence is an opinion?
qs.why: 'Best' is a feeling that cannot be proven.

qs.q: Which sentence is a fact?
qs.why: You can check that spiders have eight legs.

qs.q: Which sentence uses quotation marks correctly?
qs.why: Quotation marks surround only the spoken words.

qs.q: What should an opinion paragraph include besides your opinion?
qs.why: Reasons make an opinion convincing.

qs.q: A fact can be proven true or false.
qs.why: Facts can be checked, while opinions are beliefs.

qs.q: Match each item to its type
Put the parts of an opinion paragraph in order

learn.b: Conjunctions join words or ideas. And, but, and or join equal parts. Because, although, and when start a dependent clause. Example: I stayed in because it rained.
Present perfect uses have or has plus a past verb: 'I have finished'. Past perfect uses had: 'I had finished before dinner'. Future perfect uses will have.
An interjection shows sudden feeling, like Wow! or Oops! Use a comma after an introductory word: 'Yes, I can help.'

qs.q: Which word is a conjunction: We wanted to swim, but it was cold.
qs.why: But joins two ideas.

qs.q: Which sentence is in present perfect tense?
qs.why: Has plus eaten is present perfect.

qs.q: Which sentence is in past perfect tense?
qs.why: Had plus a past verb is past perfect.

qs.q: Which word is an interjection?
qs.why: Wow expresses sudden feeling.

qs.q: 'Because' starts a dependent clause.
qs.why: A clause starting with because cannot stand alone.

qs.q: Match each tense to an example
Put these in order of time, earliest first

learn.b: To compare characters, look at what they say, do, and feel. Ask how they are alike and different, and how each one changes.
Authors use words in creative ways. A metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human actions to objects: 'The wind whispered.' Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration.
An inference is a smart guess using clues from the text and what you know. If a character shivers and zips her coat, you can infer it is cold.

qs.q: Which sentence uses personification?
o: The sun smiled down on us.
The sun is a ball of fire.
qs.why: The sun cannot smile, so this gives it a human action.

qs.q: Which sentence is hyperbole?
o: I am so hungry I could eat a horse.
qs.why: Eating a horse is an extreme exaggeration.

qs.q: A boy slams his book and stomps away. What can you infer?
qs.why: Slamming and stomping are clues of anger.

qs.q: What is an inference?
o: A fact from the first line
qs.why: Inferences use clues plus what you already know.

qs.q: A metaphor compares two things using the word like.
qs.why: That is a simile; a metaphor says one thing is another.

qs.q: Match each device to an example
Put these steps for making an inference in order

learn.b: Writers organize information in patterns: compare and contrast, cause and effect, problem and solution, description, and sequence.
A heading names a section, a glossary defines key words, a caption explains a picture, and an index lists topics with page numbers.
Authors write to persuade, inform, or entertain. A news report informs, an advertisement persuades, and a funny story entertains.

qs.q: Where would you find the meaning of a bold word at the back of a book?
qs.why: A glossary lists and defines key words.

qs.q: A text explains how pollution leads to dying fish. Which structure is this?
qs.why: Pollution is the cause and dying fish is the effect.

qs.q: A commercial urges you to buy a toy. What is the author's purpose?
qs.why: Ads try to convince you to buy.

qs.q: What does a caption do?
qs.why: Captions sit near images and explain them.

qs.q: An index is found at the back of a book and lists topics with page numbers.
qs.why: The index helps you find topics quickly.

qs.q: Match each text structure to its clue words
Put these in order from the front to the back of a book

learn.b: A narrative tells a story with characters, a setting, and events. Use dialogue and sensory details, and use transition words like then and later.
A paragraph has a topic sentence, supporting details, and a closing sentence. Transitions like for example, however, and in conclusion connect ideas.
When you research, use more than one source and write in your own words. Never copy someone else's writing without saying where it came from. Copying is plagiarism.

qs.q: What is the topic sentence of a paragraph?
qs.why: It tells the main idea, usually at the start.

qs.q: Which transition word shows contrast?
qs.why: However introduces an opposite idea.

qs.q: What is plagiarism?
o: Copying someone's words as your own
qs.why: Plagiarism means passing off another person's work as yours.

qs.q: Which is the best way to use a source?
o: Write the ideas in your own words and name the source
qs.why: Paraphrasing and crediting is honest research.

qs.q: A narrative can include dialogue between characters.
qs.why: Dialogue makes stories more lively.

qs.q: Match each writing term to its job
Put the writing process in order

learn.b: Use I, he, she, we, they as subjects: 'She called.' Use me, him, her, us, them as objects: 'Call her.' Say 'Sam and I went', not 'Sam and me went'.
A pronoun must match the noun it replaces. 'The girls lost their bags' uses plural their for plural girls. 'Tom lost his bag' uses singular his.
Intensive pronouns end in -self or -selves and add emphasis: 'I myself cooked dinner.' You can remove them and the sentence still works.

qs.q: Which sentence is correct?
qs.why: She and I are subject pronouns.

qs.q: Choose the correct pronoun: The teacher gave the prize to ___.
qs.why: Them is the object form, used after to.

qs.q: Choose the correct pronoun: Each student must bring ___ book.
qs.why: Each is singular, so a singular pronoun fits.

qs.q: Which sentence contains an intensive pronoun?
qs.why: Herself adds emphasis to She.

qs.q: 'Them' can be the subject of a sentence.
qs.why: Them is an object pronoun; the subject form is they.

qs.q: Match each pronoun to its type
Put the steps to choose a pronoun in order
items: Check its job in the sentence

learn.b: A plot has exposition (introduction), rising action (problems grow), climax (most tense moment), falling action, and resolution (ending).
A theme is a message about life, such as 'courage means acting despite fear'. Characters change as they face the plot. Notice how they grow.
Tone is the author's attitude, like joyful or serious. Connotation is the feeling a word carries. 'Slim' feels more positive than 'skinny'.

qs.q: What is the climax of a story?
o: The most tense or important moment
qs.why: The climax is the turning point of highest tension.

qs.q: Which word has the most positive connotation?
qs.why: Determined sounds admirable, while the others sound negative.

qs.q: Which plot part comes right after the climax?
qs.why: After the climax, events wind down in the falling action.

qs.q: A story's tone is best described as
qs.why: Tone shows how the author feels about the subject.

qs.q: The resolution of a story shows how the main problem ends.
qs.why: The resolution wraps up the conflict.

qs.q: Match each plot part to its job
Put the plot parts in order

learn.b: Many English words have roots. Graph means write, so autograph is self-writing. Bio means life, so biology is the study of life. Port means carry, so transport means carry across.
Denotation is the dictionary meaning. Connotation is the emotion attached to a word. Both 'house' and 'home' mean a place to live, but 'home' feels warmer.
An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not literal. 'Break the ice' means to start a friendly conversation. 'Piece of cake' means very easy.

qs.q: The root 'bio' means life. What is biology?
qs.why: Bio means life and -logy means study of.

qs.q: What does the idiom 'piece of cake' mean?
qs.why: It is an idiom meaning something is easy.

qs.q: The root 'port' means carry. What does 'transport' mean?
qs.why: Trans means across and port means carry.

qs.q: What is a word's denotation?
qs.why: Denotation is the literal meaning.

qs.q: An idiom means exactly what its words say.
qs.why: Idioms have a meaning that differs from the literal words.

qs.q: Match each root to its meaning
Put these steps for figuring out a new word in order

learn.b: A claim is the point you argue, like 'Schools should start later.' Evidence is facts, examples, or data that support it. Reasoning explains why the evidence proves the claim.
A summary tells only the main points in your own words, without your opinion. It is much shorter than the original text.
In formal writing, avoid slang and contractions like gonna. Use clear sentences and precise words. Keep the tone respectful.

qs.q: What is a claim in an argument?
qs.why: The claim is the position you try to prove.

qs.q: Which is the best evidence for the claim 'Exercise helps health'?
o: A study shows exercise lowers heart disease risk.
qs.why: A study gives a checkable fact.

qs.q: Which is true about a good summary?
o: It uses the main points in your own words
It is longer than the text
qs.why: Summaries are short and objective.

qs.q: Which sentence is the most formal?
o: Students need adequate sleep to learn well.
qs.why: It avoids slang and is clear and precise.

qs.q: A summary should include your personal opinions.
qs.why: A summary only restates the text's main ideas.

qs.q: Match each argument part to its job
Put the parts of an argument essay in order

learn.b: A clause has a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand alone: 'I read.' A dependent clause cannot: 'when I read'. A phrase lacks a subject or verb.
A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound has two joined by a conjunction like and or but. A complex has an independent plus a dependent clause.
Use a comma and a conjunction to join two clauses: 'I was tired, but I finished.' A semicolon can join two related independent clauses: 'I was tired; I finished.'

qs.q: Which is a dependent clause?
qs.why: It has a subject and verb but cannot stand alone.

qs.q: Which sentence is compound?
o: I like tea, and she likes coffee.
qs.why: It joins two independent clauses with and.

qs.q: Which sentence is complex?
o: I ran because I was late.
I ran, she walked, we met.
qs.why: Because I was late is a dependent clause attached to an independent one.

qs.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
o: I was cold; I put on a coat.
Although; I was cold, I stayed.
qs.why: A semicolon joins two complete, related sentences.

qs.q: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence.
qs.why: It has a subject and verb and expresses a complete thought.

qs.q: Match each sentence type to an example
Put the steps to check a sentence in order

learn.b: A theme grows through the whole story. Look at conflicts, how the main character changes, and repeated ideas. The theme is a statement, such as 'Pride can lead to loss'.
First person gives us only the narrator's thoughts. Third person limited follows one character's thoughts. Third person omniscient knows what all characters think.
Character vs. character, character vs. self (inner struggle), character vs. nature, and character vs. society are the main types of conflict.

qs.q: A character struggles with her own fear. What type of conflict is this?
qs.why: The struggle happens inside her.

qs.q: A narrator who knows every character's thoughts is
qs.why: Omniscient means all-knowing.

qs.q: Which is written as a theme statement?
qs.why: A theme is a full statement about life, not just a topic.

qs.q: A hiker fights a blizzard. What type of conflict is this?
qs.why: The hiker struggles against a natural force.

qs.q: In first-person point of view, the narrator uses the word I.
qs.why: First person means the narrator is a character telling the story.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these steps for finding a theme in order
items: State the theme as a sentence

learn.b: Alliteration repeats starting sounds: 'silly snakes slither'. Onomatopoeia imitates sounds, like buzz or crash. An allusion refers to a famous story or person. An idiom has a non-literal meaning.
Words can be linked as synonyms, antonyms, or by degree. 'Glance', 'look', and 'stare' show growing intensity. Analogies show these links: hot is to cold as up is to down.
Context clues can be definitions, examples, or contrasts. In 'The tranquil lake, calm and still, soothed us', the words calm and still define tranquil.

qs.q: Which phrase is an example of alliteration?
qs.why: The repeated p sound is alliteration.

qs.q: Which word is onomatopoeia?
qs.why: Sizzle imitates the sound it names.

qs.q: What does 'tranquil' mean: The tranquil lake, calm and still, soothed us?
qs.why: Calm and still are context clues.

qs.q: Hot is to cold as up is to ___.
qs.why: Both pairs are antonyms.

qs.q: An allusion refers to a well-known person, story, or event.
qs.why: Example: calling someone a Romeo alludes to Romeo and Juliet.

qs.q: Match each device to its example
Put these from least to most intense

learn.b: A thesis states your main argument in one sentence. 'Schools should offer more art classes because art builds creativity' is clear and arguable.
Good sources are accurate, current, and by experts. Check the author and the date. Be careful with sources that show bias or have no author.
Paraphrase means restating an idea in your own words, and you still must credit the source. A direct quote uses quotation marks and the exact words.

qs.q: Which is the strongest thesis statement?
o: Shelter dogs make loyal pets, so families should adopt them.
qs.why: It makes a clear, arguable claim with a reason.

qs.q: Which source is most reliable for facts about space?
qs.why: NASA is an expert, trustworthy organization.

qs.q: What is paraphrasing?
o: Restating an idea in your own words
qs.why: A paraphrase keeps the meaning but changes the wording.

qs.q: When should you use quotation marks?
o: For the exact words of a source
qs.why: Quotation marks show exact words from someone else.

qs.q: You must credit a source even when you paraphrase it.
qs.why: The ideas still belong to the original author.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the research steps in order

learn.b: Verbals look like verbs but act as other parts of speech. A gerund ends in -ing and acts as a noun: 'Swimming is fun.' An infinitive is to plus a verb: 'I want to swim.' A participle acts as an adjective: 'the broken window'.
In active voice the subject does the action: 'Maya threw the ball.' In passive voice the subject receives it: 'The ball was thrown by Maya.' Active voice is usually clearer.
Indicative mood states facts: 'She is here.' Imperative gives commands: 'Sit down.' Subjunctive shows wishes or unreal things: 'If I were you, I would wait.'

qs.q: Which word is a gerund in: Reading improves your mind?
qs.why: Reading is an -ing word acting as a noun.

qs.q: Which sentence is in passive voice?
o: Dinner was cooked by the chef.
qs.why: The subject, dinner, receives the action.

qs.q: Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood?
o: If I were rich, I would travel.
qs.why: 'If I were' expresses a wish or unreal situation.

qs.q: Which is an infinitive?
qs.why: An infinitive is to plus the base verb.

qs.q: 'Close the window' is in the imperative mood.
qs.why: Imperative sentences give commands.

qs.q: Match each term to an example
Put the steps to turn passive into active in order

learn.b: Poems use stanzas (groups of lines), rhyme, rhythm, and imagery. Free verse has no regular rhyme or meter. Imagery uses the senses to paint a picture.

Verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant: 'Great weather!' during a storm. Situational irony is when the outcome is opposite to what is expected. Dramatic irony is when readers know something a character does not.
Mood is the feeling the reader gets. Tone is the author's attitude. A symbol is an object that stands for an idea, like a dove for peace.

qs.q: A fire station burns down. What kind of irony is this?
qs.why: The outcome is the opposite of what we expect.

qs.q: What is a stanza?
o: A group of lines in a poem
qs.why: Stanzas are like paragraphs in poetry.

qs.q: A dove often symbolizes
qs.why: Doves are a common symbol of peace.

qs.q: What is free verse?
o: Poetry with no regular rhyme or rhythm
qs.why: Free verse does not follow set patterns.

qs.q: Mood is the feeling a reader gets from a text.
qs.why: Mood describes the atmosphere, such as eerie or cheerful.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these steps for analyzing a poem in order

learn.b: The central idea is the main point of a text. Authors support it with claims and evidence. Ask whether the evidence is relevant and enough.
Ethos appeals to credibility, logos to logic and facts, and pathos to emotions. A doctor citing studies uses ethos and logos. A touching story about a sad puppy uses pathos.
Bias is a one-sided view. A logical fallacy is faulty reasoning, like a bandwagon claim: 'Everyone buys it, so it must be good.' Always check if the evidence really proves the point.

qs.q: An ad uses a sad puppy to get donations. Which appeal is this?
qs.why: Pathos appeals to emotions.

qs.q: A speaker lists statistics to prove a point. Which appeal is this?
qs.why: Logos appeals to logic and data.

qs.q: 'Everyone is buying it, so it must be great' is an example of
qs.why: Popularity does not prove quality.

qs.q: What does ethos rely on?
qs.why: Ethos builds trust through credentials or character.

qs.q: A biased text presents only one side of an issue.
qs.why: Bias means leaning unfairly toward one view.

qs.q: Match each appeal to its focus
Put the steps to evaluate an argument in order

learn.b: A strong argument has a clear claim, reasons backed by evidence, and a response to the opposing view (a counterclaim). End by restating your claim.
Narratives use dialogue, pacing, description, and reflection. Slow down important moments with detail, and speed through unimportant ones.
Revising improves ideas, order, and word choice. Editing fixes spelling, grammar, and punctuation. Do revising first, then editing.

qs.q: What is a counterclaim?
qs.why: A counterclaim is the other side's argument, which you answer.

qs.q: Which should you do first?
qs.why: Revise big ideas before fixing small errors.

qs.q: Which technique slows down a key moment in a narrative?
qs.why: Detail stretches time and builds tension.

qs.q: A strong argument ends with
o: A restated claim and closing thought
qs.why: The conclusion reinforces the claim.

qs.q: Editing means fixing spelling, grammar, and punctuation.
qs.why: Editing deals with surface errors.

qs.q: Match each writing job to its type
Put the writing process in order

learn.b: Stories are built from plot, conflict, setting, and characters. A round character is complex, while a flat character has few traits. A dynamic character changes over time; a static one does not.
A symbol is an object or image that stands for a larger idea, like a green light meaning hope. A motif is a repeated element, such as recurring images of darkness, that supports the theme.
An archetype is a pattern found in many stories, such as the hero's journey or the wise mentor. An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known work, person, or event.

qs.q: A character who changes significantly during a story is called
qs.why: Dynamic characters undergo real change.

qs.q: A repeated image that supports the theme is a
qs.why: A motif is a recurring element that builds meaning.

qs.q: Calling a traitor 'a Judas' is an example of
qs.why: It refers to the biblical figure Judas.

qs.q: A wise old mentor who guides a young hero is an example of a(n)
qs.why: Mentors appear in many stories as an archetype.

qs.q: A static character stays basically the same throughout a story.
qs.why: Static means unchanging.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the parts of plot in order

learn.b: A Shakespearean sonnet has 14 lines and rhymes ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. Iambic pentameter has five pairs of syllables per line, unstressed then stressed, like da-DUM da-DUM.
In a soliloquy a character speaks thoughts aloud while alone on stage. An aside is a short remark to the audience that other characters do not hear. Both reveal hidden feelings.
A tragedy is a drama in which the main character, often with a flaw, suffers a downfall or death. Romeo and Juliet and Macbeth are Shakespearean tragedies.

qs.q: How many lines are in a Shakespearean sonnet?
qs.why: Sonnets always have 14 lines.

qs.q: A character alone on stage speaks his thoughts aloud. This is a
qs.why: A soliloquy reveals inner thoughts to the audience.

qs.q: Iambic pentameter has how many stressed syllables per line?
qs.why: Penta means five feet, each with one stress.

qs.q: Which play is a Shakespearean tragedy?
qs.why: Hamlet ends with the downfall and death of its hero.

qs.q: An aside is a remark that the other characters on stage cannot hear.
qs.why: It is aimed at the audience.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these steps for analyzing a poem in order

learn.b: Items in a list should have the same form. Write 'I like swimming, running, and hiking', not 'swimming, to run, and hikes'. Parallel structure makes writing smooth.

A modifier should be next to what it describes. 'Running down the street, the bus hit him' is a dangling modifier because the bus was not running. Fix: 'Running down the street, he was hit by the bus.'
Use a semicolon between two related independent clauses. Use a colon after a complete sentence to introduce a list or explanation. Use commas around nonessential phrases.

qs.q: Which sentence has parallel structure?
o: She likes to read, writing, and to swim.
She likes reading, writing, and swimming.
She likes read, write, and swimming.

learn.b: A literary analysis begins with a thesis about how the author uses a technique to create meaning. Support it with quotes and explain each one.
Introduce a quote with a short lead-in, put the exact words in quotation marks, and explain it afterward. This 'quote sandwich' keeps your analysis clear.
Think about audience and purpose. Persuasive writing uses ethos, pathos, and logos. Academic writing uses formal tone and avoids slang.

learn.b: Every text has an author, an audience, and a purpose. Good writers adjust word choice and tone to fit them. A letter to a principal sounds different from a text to a friend.
Ethos builds trust, pathos stirs emotion, and logos uses logic and evidence. Strong arguments often combine all three.
Repetition stresses an idea. Parallelism gives rhythm. A rhetorical question makes the audience think, and antithesis sets up contrast: 'Ask not what your country can do for you.'

qs.q: A speaker lists her medical degrees to gain trust. Which appeal is this?
qs.why: Credentials build credibility, which is ethos.

qs.why: Pathos aims at feelings such as pity or fear.

learn.b: Authors from many cultures explore the same big ideas: power, identity, justice, and survival. Comparing texts shows how different writers treat one theme.
Satire uses humor and exaggeration to criticize people or society. Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal and George Orwell's Animal Farm are famous satires.
An allegory is a story whose characters and events stand for deeper meanings. A dystopia shows a frightening society, as in Orwell's 1984.

qs.why: Satire mocks faults to encourage change.

learn.b: Knowing roots helps decode hard words. Bene means good (benefit), mal means bad (malice), and spec means look (inspect). Prefixes and suffixes change meaning and part of speech.
Diction is the author's word choice. Words with similar meanings can feel different: 'thrifty' sounds good, 'stingy' sounds bad. Careful diction shapes tone.
Syntax is how words are arranged in sentences. Mixing short and long sentences keeps writing lively. A short sentence after a long one can create emphasis.

qs.q: The root 'bene' means good. What does 'benefit' most likely mean?
qs.why: Bene points to something good.

qs.why: Stingy suggests selfishness with money.

qs.q: Syntax refers to how words are arranged in sentences.
qs.why: Syntax covers sentence structure and word order.

learn.b: State a debatable claim, support it with reasons and evidence, answer counterarguments, and finish with a conclusion. Use credible sources and cite them.
Check the author's expertise, the publisher, the date, and whether other sources agree. Primary sources are first-hand records, like letters. Secondary sources interpret them.
MLA and APA are common citation styles. A works cited or reference list gives full details of each source. In-text citations point readers to it. Always credit borrowed ideas.

qs.q: Which is a primary source?
o: A diary written during World War II
qs.why: A diary is a first-hand record from the time.

o: An expert author and cited sources

qs.q: You should cite a source even when you paraphrase it.
qs.why: The ideas belong to the original author.

learn.b: Early American writers like William Bradford and Anne Bradstreet wrote plain, religious works. Jonathan Edwards preached the famous sermon 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'. Themes were faith, duty, and God's judgment.

The Enlightenment valued reason. Benjamin Franklin wrote practical essays and an autobiography. Thomas Paine's Common Sense and Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence used clear arguments to support revolution.
Romantic writers like Poe and Hawthorne explored emotion and the dark side of human nature. Transcendentalists such as Emerson and Thoreau valued nature, individualism, and intuition.

qs.q: Who wrote 'Common Sense' to urge American independence?
qs.why: Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet argued for independence.

qs.why: Transcendentalists trusted the individual and valued nature.

learn.b: After the Civil War, writers like Mark Twain and Stephen Crane showed ordinary life and regional speech. Realism describes life as it is. Naturalism adds that nature and environment control people's fate.

After World War I, writers like F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway, and T. S. Eliot broke old forms. Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby critiques the American Dream. Hemingway used short, plain sentences.
In the 1920s, Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, and Claude McKay celebrated Black culture and voices. Later writers like Arthur Miller and Harper Lee explored justice and society.

qs.why: F. Scott Fitzgerald published it in 1925.

qs.why: Hughes was a central poet of the movement.

learn.b: Find the claim, the reasons, and the evidence. Then judge the author's choices: how appeals, tone, and organization help persuade the audience.

A straw man misstates the other side to attack it. An ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument. A false dilemma offers only two choices when more exist. A slippery slope claims one step will lead to disaster.
Diction, syntax, and imagery create tone. Short sentences can feel urgent, long ones thoughtful. Notice shifts in tone, which often signal a change in the author's argument.

learn.b: Synthesis means combining ideas from several sources to support your own argument. Do not just summarize each source one by one. Use them together to build a point.
A college essay tells a true story about you, shows who you are, and reflects on what you learned. Use specific details and a natural voice. Avoid cliches.
Cut wordiness, use strong verbs, and vary sentence length. Replace 'is' and 'are' with active verbs where you can. Read your work aloud to hear awkward spots.

qs.why: Synthesis blends sources to support your argument.

learn.b: Beowulf is an Old English epic poem about a hero fighting monsters. Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales (about 1400) tells stories of pilgrims traveling to Canterbury in Middle English.
Shakespeare wrote plays like Hamlet and Macbeth and many sonnets. Writers like Christopher Marlowe and John Donne also thrived. English began to look more like the language we use today.
John Milton wrote the epic Paradise Lost. In the 1700s, Jonathan Swift wrote satires like Gulliver's Travels, and Alexander Pope used witty verse. Satire criticized society.

learn.b: Romantic poets like Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats, and Shelley valued emotion, imagination, and nature. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is a Gothic Romantic novel about the dangers of unchecked science.
Under Queen Victoria, Charles Dickens (Great Expectations) exposed poverty and injustice. The Bronte sisters wrote Jane Eyre and Wuthering Heights. Many novels were published in serial parts.

Modernists like Virginia Woolf used stream of consciousness to show a character's thoughts. George Orwell wrote 1984 about totalitarian control. Post-war writers explored identity, empire, and society.

learn.b: A critical lens is a way of reading a text. A historical lens looks at the time it was written. A feminist lens looks at gender roles. A psychological lens looks at the characters' minds and motives.
Close reading means reading slowly and noticing details: word choice, imagery, structure, and tone. Ask why the author made each choice and what effect it has.
An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted, which makes readers question the story. Structure choices like flashbacks, frame stories, and nonlinear time shape meaning.

learn.b: A research paper asks a focused question, gathers credible sources, and builds an argument with evidence. Use a consistent citation style and a works cited page.
Resumes list skills and experience briefly. Cover letters explain why you fit a job. Emails should have a clear subject, a polite tone, and be short and specific.
Good speakers know their audience, organize points clearly, make eye contact, and speak at a steady pace. Visuals should support, not replace, what you say.
